units.title: Hello, Objective-C!
units.summary: Write your first Objective-C program, print text and numbers with printf and send your first message to an object.

lesson.md: Objective-C is the C language plus **objects** and **messages**. For many years it was the main language for apps on Apple platforms, and a lot of code still uses it. A source file ends in `.m`, and every program starts in a function called `main`.

Line by line: `#import <Foundation/Foundation.h>` loads **Foundation**, Apple's basic library with strings, numbers and lists. `int main(void)` defines the function `main`, where the program starts. `int` means that it gives back a whole number, and `void` means that it takes no input.

`@autoreleasepool { }` marks the area where the program creates objects; Foundation cleans them up at its end. Put your code inside it. `return 0;` tells the system that the program ended without an error. Code blocks go between the braces `{` and `}`, and every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
`printf` comes from C. It prints the text between the double quotes. It does not start a new line by itself: `\n` inside the text is the **new line** character.

`printf` can also fill in values. Each placeholder in the text takes the next value after the comma: `%d` for a whole number and `%f` for a decimal number. `%.2f` shows exactly two digits after the decimal point. Without quotes, `2 + 3` is a calculation; `*` multiplies and `/` divides.

Text with an `@` in front, like `@"Hi"`, is an Objective-C string object of the class `NSString`. You talk to an object by sending it a **message** in square brackets: `[object message]`. `printf` cannot print an `NSString` directly. The message `UTF8String` gives back the text in the C form that the placeholder `%s` expects.

In other Objective-C code you will often see `NSLog(@"Hi")`. `NSLog` writes to the error output and adds the date, the time and the program name to every line. That is why this course prints with `printf`.
Objective-C is case sensitive: `printf` works, `Printf` does not. A missing `;` is an error. A line that starts with `//` is a comment, and the compiler ignores it.

card: `[@"Hi" UTF8String]` sends a message; print it with `%s`

units.title: Variables and types
units.summary: Store values in variables and meet int, double, BOOL, NSString and NSNumber.

lesson.md: A **variable** stores a value under a name. In Objective-C you write the type first, then the name: `int age = 30;`. `int` holds whole numbers and `double` holds decimal numbers. The `=` puts a value into the variable, and you can change it later.

You can calculate with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`. When you divide two `int` values, the result is an `int` too, and the part after the point is dropped. `%` gives the **remainder** of a division. If one of the numbers is a `double`, like `7.0`, the result is a `double`.
The type `BOOL` stores a truth value: `YES` or `NO`. With `%d`, `printf` prints `1` for `YES` and `0` for `NO`. A comparison like `10 > 3` also gives a truth value.

`int`, `double` and `BOOL` are plain values from C. Objects work differently: an object lives somewhere in memory, and the variable stores a **pointer**, the address of the object. That is what the `*` in `NSString *name` means. You write it for every object variable.

`NSNumber` puts a number into an object. `@42`, `@0.25` and `@YES` create `NSNumber` objects. You get the plain value back with the messages `intValue`, `doubleValue` and `boolValue`. You will need `NSNumber` for lists, because they can only store objects.
Put `const` before the type for a value that never changes: `const int limit = 10;`. If you try to change `limit` later, the program does not compile.
Do not forget the `@` before an Objective-C string: `NSString *name = "Ada";` is an error, because `"Ada"` without `@` is a plain C text. Without the `*`, `NSString name` is an error too.

card: `NSString *s = @"Hi";` stores a pointer to an object

units.title: Strings
units.summary: Work with NSString: length, upper case, joining, stringWithFormat: and comparing text.

lesson.md: An `NSString` never changes after you create it. Its methods give you **new** strings instead. The message `length` gives the number of characters, and `uppercaseString` and `lowercaseString` give copies in capital or small letters.

`length` gives back an `NSUInteger`, a whole number that is never negative. Print it with `%lu`. In `[[word lowercaseString] UTF8String]` the inner message runs first, and the outer message is sent to its result.

Some messages need a value. The value comes after a colon: `[first stringByAppendingString:@" morning"]`. The colon is part of the message name `stringByAppendingString:`. The result is a new string, and `first` stays the same.

`[NSString stringWithFormat:...]` builds a new string from a format, like `printf`. Here the message goes to the class `NSString` itself, not to a string. The placeholders are the same as in `printf`, plus `%@` for any object, for example an `NSString` or an `NSNumber`.
`[a isEqualToString:b]` compares the text of two strings and gives back a `BOOL`. `hasPrefix:` checks the start of a string, and `containsString:` looks for a text anywhere inside it.
Do not compare strings with `==`. It only checks whether both pointers point to the same object, not whether the texts are the same. Use `isEqualToString:`.
`%@` only works in `stringWithFormat:` (and `NSLog`). `printf` does not know objects, so print strings there with `%s` and `UTF8String`.

units.title: Decisions
units.summary: Let your program decide with if, else, switch, logical operators and BOOL values.

lesson.md: `if (condition) { ... }` runs the code in the braces only when the condition is true. Conditions often compare values: `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.
`else` runs when the condition is false. With `else if` you can check more conditions one after the other. Only the first block whose condition is true runs.

`&&` means **and**: both sides must be true. `||` means **or**: at least one side must be true. `!` means **not** and turns true into false. A `BOOL` can be the whole condition, like `if (member)`. As in C, `0` counts as false and every other number counts as true.
`switch` compares a whole number with several `case` values. `break` leaves the `switch`. Without `break`, the program continues with the next `case`. `default` runs when no `case` matches.
The **conditional operator** `condition ? a : b` gives `a` when the condition is true and `b` otherwise. It is a short form of a small `if`/`else`.
`=` stores a value, `==` compares. `if (x = 5)` stores `5` in `x`, and the condition is always true. The compiler warns you about this.
`switch` only works with whole numbers. To compare strings, use `if` with `isEqualToString:`.

units.title: Loops
units.summary: Repeat code with for and while, control loops with break and continue, and walk through lists with for-in.

lesson.md: A `for` loop repeats code. Its header has three parts, separated by `;`: the start (`int i = 1`), the condition (`i <= 3`) and the step (`i++`). The loop runs as long as the condition is true. `i++` adds 1 to `i`.
The step can be anything. `i -= 3` makes `i` smaller by 3, `i--` subtracts 1. In the same way, `+=` adds to a variable: `total += 5` is the same as `total = total + 5`.
A `while` loop repeats as long as its condition is true. It checks the condition before every round. Make sure that something in the loop changes the condition, or the loop never ends.
`continue` skips the rest of the current round and starts the next one. `break` leaves the loop at once.

`for (NSString *w in words)` goes through every object in a collection, from the first to the last. This is called **fast enumeration**. `@[...]` creates an array, a list of objects; the next unit explains arrays in detail.
A common pattern: start with a total of `0` and add every item in the loop. The numbers in an array are `NSNumber` objects, so you need `intValue`.

units.title: Arrays and dictionaries
units.summary: Store objects in NSArray and NSDictionary, change them with the mutable versions and read them with subscripts.

lesson.md: An `NSArray` is an ordered list of objects. `@[...]` creates one. `count` gives the number of items, and `fruits[0]` reads an item by its **index**. The first index is `0`.

Arrays only store objects, so numbers go in as `NSNumber`, like `@10`. `containsObject:` checks whether an item is in the array. An index that does not exist, like `fruits[3]`, stops the program with an error.

An `NSArray` never changes. An `NSMutableArray` can: `addObject:` adds an item at the end, `removeObjectAtIndex:` removes one, and `list[0] = ...` replaces one. `[NSMutableArray array]` creates an empty mutable array.

An `NSDictionary` stores pairs of a **key** and a **value**. `@{key: value, ...}` creates one, and `ages[@"Ada"]` reads the value for a key. For a key that is not there, you get `nil`, which means "no object".
An `NSMutableDictionary` can change: `stock[@"apple"] = @5` adds a pair, or replaces the value if the key is already there. A dictionary has no fixed order, so do not rely on the order of its keys.
A message to `nil` does nothing and gives back `0` or `nil`. So `[ages[@"Bob"] intValue]` is `0` and does not stop the program.
You cannot add to an array created with `@[...]`: `addObject:` only exists for `NSMutableArray`. Collections also cannot store `nil` or plain numbers like `5`; use `@5`.

units.title: Classes
units.summary: Define your own classes with @interface and @implementation, write methods and create objects with alloc and init.

lesson.md: A **class** is a plan for objects. It has two parts. The `@interface` lists what objects of the class can do. The `@implementation` contains the code of the **methods**. Both parts end with `@end`. `Dog : NSObject` means that `Dog` is based on `NSObject`, the base class of almost all classes.

`[[Dog alloc] init]` creates an object: `alloc` reserves memory, and `init` prepares the new object. The `-` before a method makes it an **instance method**, a method you send to an object. `(void)` means that the method gives back nothing. **ARC** (Automatic Reference Counting) frees the memory of an object automatically when nobody uses it anymore.

The type in parentheses after `-` is what the method gives back, and `return` gives it back. Each parameter comes after a colon: `- (int)add:(int)a to:(int)b` has the name `add:to:` and takes two `int` values. A method with `+` is a **class method**: you send it to the class itself, like `[Calculator square:7]` or `[NSString stringWithFormat:...]`.

An object can store its own data in **instance variables**. You declare them in braces after `@implementation`. Their names usually start with `_`. Every object has its own copy, and it starts at `0` (or `nil` for objects).

To give an object values when you create it, write your own `init` method. `self` is the object itself, and `[super init]` runs the `init` of `NSObject` first. If that worked, `self` is not `nil`, and you store the values. `instancetype` means "an object of this class".

A method in the `@interface` ends with `;`, the same method in the `@implementation` has its code in braces. An instance method needs an object: `[Dog bark]` does not work when `bark` is a `-` method.

units.title: Properties and blocks
units.summary: Declare properties, use dot syntax, understand messages and store code in blocks.

lesson.md: Writing an instance variable plus methods to read and change it takes many lines. `@property` does it for you: `@property int age;` creates the storage, a **getter** `age` to read it and a **setter** `setAge:` to change it.

The **dot syntax** is a short form for these messages: `p.age` is the same as `[p age]`, and `p.age = 40` is the same as `[p setAge:40]`. The setter name is `set` plus the property name with a capital first letter.

Properties can have **attributes** in parentheses. `nonatomic` is the usual choice in apps. `copy` keeps its own copy of a string. `readonly` creates only a getter. Inside the class, you reach a property with `self`, for example `self.width`. You can also write the getter yourself, like `area` here.

Every `[object message]` is a message. The object decides while the program runs which method answers it. `@selector(name)` stands for a message name, and `respondsToSelector:` asks an object whether it understands that message. A message to `nil` does nothing and gives back `0`.

A **block** is a piece of code that you can store in a variable and run later, like a small function without a name. `^` starts a block. In `int (^square)(int)`, the variable `square` holds a block that takes an `int` and gives back an `int`. You run it with parentheses: `square(6)`.

A block can use variables from outside. It keeps the value they had when the block was created. Many Foundation methods take a block, for example `enumerateObjectsUsingBlock:`, which runs the block for every item of an array together with its index.
The `stop` parameter lets you end the enumeration early: set `*stop = YES;` inside the block. To change an outside variable inside a block, declare it with `__block`, like `__block int total = 0;`.
